answer:
At 1 atm, a liquid of 95 mol% ethanol and 5 mol% water is in equilibrium with a vapour of about **94.6 mol% ethanol and 5.4 mol% water**. The bubble point is about **78.3 °C**.

The vapour holds slightly less ethanol than the liquid because 95% is past the ethanol–water azeotrope. Above that point water is the more volatile component, so ordinary distillation cannot push ethanol beyond the azeotrope.

I computed this, not recalled it. I used a bubble-point calculation with modified Raoult's law (ideal vapour, liquid activity coefficients) in the `thermo` Python package, which supplied the vapour pressures. Three activity models agree:

| Model | Bubble T (°C) | y ethanol | γ ethanol | γ water |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NRTL (ChemSep parameters) | 78.26 | 0.9455 | 1.001 | 2.50 |
| Modified UNIFAC (Dortmund) | 78.30 | 0.9467 | 1.001 | 2.44 |
| Original UNIFAC | 78.22 | 0.9449 | 1.003 | 2.53 |

As a sanity check, the NRTL model puts the azeotrope at about x = y ≈ 0.885–0.89 ethanol and 78.18 °C. From memory, the usual literature value is 0.894 at 78.15 °C; I did not check that against a source, and I did not compare the 95% point against measured data. The spread between the three models (about ±0.001 in y) gives a rough idea of the uncertainty.
